facts.a: Tipo 00 refers to how finely the flour is milled - the finest Italian grade - not to its protein content. For Neapolitan pizza you want a 00 flour that is also reasonably strong: around 11 to 13 percent protein, W strength 250 to 320. The fine grind gives that silky, extensible dough that stretches paper thin without tearing.
alt: The 00 is a milling grade, the finest in the Italian system - it says nothing about strength by itself. Pick a 00 milled for pizza: medium-strong, W 250-320. Caputo's blue Pizzeria bag is the classic example.

It's the finest Italian mill grade. People think 00 means 'pizza flour' automatically, but a weak 00 cake flour would collapse in a long fermentation. You want fine milling AND enough protein, roughly 11-13 percent.

People hear 'tipo 00' and assume it means high-protein pizza flour. It does not - 00 is purely the milling grade, the finest sieve in the Italian system, and a 00 can be weak pastry flour or strong pizza flour. Look for both on the bag: fine milling plus 11-13 percent protein, W 250-320. Fineness gives the silky stretch; strength lets the dough survive a long fermentation.

facts.a: W is the flour strength index measured with a Chopin alveograph - it inflates a bubble of dough and measures the work needed to burst it. Higher W means more gluten strength and more fermentation tolerance. For a same-day pizza dough, W 200-250 suffices; for 24-48 hour fermentations you want W 280-320; very long ferments push toward W 350.
alt: It's a lab measure of dough strength: a machine blows the dough into a bubble and records the energy to break it. Practical rule: match W to fermentation time. Short proof, W around 220. Two-day cold ferment, W 300ish. The longer the ferment, the stronger the flour must be to hold its structure.

Do not read W as the protein percentage, even though the two travel together. It is the alveograph's strength index - the energy needed to blow a dough bubble until it bursts - and it tells you how long a dough can ferment before it collapses. A W 200-250 flour is right for a same-day dough; W 280-320 for 24-48 hours; only very long ferments justify W 350.

Stronger is not automatically better - that is the mistake I see most. A W 350 flour in a four-hour dough gives you a tough, rubbery base that fights the stretch, because the gluten never got the time it was built for. Match the number to your schedule: W 200-250 same day, W 280-320 for a two-day ferment, W 350 only for very long maturations.

facts.a: Classic Neapolitan runs 55 to 62 percent hydration - lower than people expect. The tenderness comes from the fierce 90-second bake, not from a wet dough. Modern 'contemporary Neapolitan' pizzerias push 65-70 percent for an even airier cornicione, but the traditional AVPN dough sits under 63.

People assume Neapolitan must be a high-hydration dough, and they are wrong. Traditional dough sits at 55 to 62 percent - drier than most artisan bread. The pillowy texture is the work of a 90-second bake at ferocious heat, which steams the crumb before it can dry out. Only the contemporary canotto school runs 65-70 percent, and that is a modern departure, not the canon.

Fifty-five to sixty-two percent for the classic article, and I would start at 60 if you are new to it. If someone tells you real Neapolitan dough is 70 percent, they are describing the contemporary puffy-rim style, not the AVPN tradition, which stays under 63. A drier dough is easier to handle in a home oven, too.

alt: About 55 percent, plus a little olive or seed oil. Dry dough, thin roll, longer bake: that's the crunch formula. Don't confuse it with Roman al taglio, which goes as wet as 85 percent - same city, opposite philosophy.

Drier than you think, and definitely drier than Neapolitan: Roman tonda sits around 55 percent hydration with a little oil. If someone tells you Roman pizza is a wet dough, they are thinking of al taglio - the tray pizza at 75 to 90 percent. Tonda and al taglio share a city and nothing else in the mixing bowl.

Around 55 percent, and that dry dough is the point - more water does not mean more crunch. A wet dough stays tender inside; a tight 55 percent dough rolled thin and baked longer at a gentler heat dries all the way through into a cracker. Al taglio is the wet cousin at 75-90 percent, built for an open crumb, not for snap.

facts.a: Two and a half to three percent of the flour weight - for a kilo of flour, 25 to 30 grams. Neapolitan tradition runs saltier than most bread. Salt tightens the gluten and slows the yeast, which is part of the dough's structure, so don't cut it without adjusting the fermentation.
alt: Baker's math: 2.5-3 percent of flour weight. It's not just seasoning - salt strengthens gluten and brakes the yeast. Cut the salt and your dough both tastes flat and overproofs faster.

Twenty-five to thirty grams per kilo of flour - 2.5 to 3 percent. Do not confuse that figure with the yeast: the yeast is the tiny one at one to three grams per kilo, the salt is the generous one. Salt is not only seasoning; it tightens gluten and slows the yeast, so halving it changes both the taste and the fermentation clock.

Salt is not just for taste, and a pinch is not enough. Neapolitan dough runs 2.5 to 3 percent of flour weight - 25 to 30 grams for a kilo - which is saltier than most bread. That salt firms the gluten so the dough stretches thin without tearing, and it reins the yeast in so a long ferment does not run away. Cut it and you pay twice: flat flavor, faster overproof.

facts.a: Almost comically little: for a long-fermented Neapolitan dough, one to three grams of fresh yeast per kilo of flour - a pea-sized amount. Time does the work that extra yeast would rush. If a recipe calls for a whole sachet of yeast and a one-hour rise, it's making bread-shaped disappointment, not pizza.
alt: A gram or two of fresh yeast per kilo of flour for a 24-hour ferment. That's the whole secret of digestible pizza: minimal yeast, maximum time. Fast doughs with seven grams of yeast are why bad pizza sits in your stomach like a stone.

One to three grams of fresh yeast per kilo of flour for a long ferment - and no, that is not a typo, and it is not the salt figure. Salt is the big number at 25-30 grams per kilo; yeast is the pea-sized one. A whole 7 gram sachet is a bread habit: it rushes the rise, skips the flavor, and leaves you with a dough that sits heavy.

More yeast is not better, it is only faster - and fast is the enemy of good pizza. For a Neapolitan dough fermented 24 hours, one to three grams of fresh yeast per kilo of flour is plenty; the time does the leavening. Heavy-yeast doughs taste yeasty, brown poorly, and are the reason people think pizza is hard to digest.

facts.a: True Neapolitan dough contains no oil and no sugar - the STG specification allows only flour, water, salt, and yeast. Oil isn't needed because the bake is too fast for the crust to dry out. Roman and New York doughs add oil precisely because their longer, cooler bakes would otherwise turn the crust hard instead of crisp.
alt: No. Four ingredients, and oil is not one of them. Oil belongs in doughs that bake long and relatively cool - Roman tonda, teglia, New York - where it keeps the crumb tender. At 450 degrees for 90 seconds, oil would just be lost.

People will tell you every Italian pizza dough has olive oil in it. Neapolitan does not - the STG spec lists flour, water, salt and yeast, and nothing else, no oil and no sugar. The oil habit belongs to Rome, where tonda dough takes a spoonful because its longer, cooler bake would otherwise dry the crust hard. Put the good oil on top after the bake instead.

Not in Naples. A 450-degree, 90-second bake never dries the crust, so oil has no job to do and the tradition simply left it out. Roman tonda, teglia and New York all bake longer and cooler, and there oil keeps the crumb tender instead of tough. If your dough is Neapolitan, it is four ingredients; if it has oil in it, call it something else.

facts.a: Cold fermentation - 24 to 72 hours at around 4 degrees Celsius - slows the yeast to a crawl while enzymes keep working, breaking starches into sugars and proteins into flavor compounds. The result: complex, slightly tangy flavor, better browning from the freed sugars, and a more digestible, extensible dough. It's the single biggest upgrade a home pizza maker can adopt.
alt: It separates flavor development from gas production. At fridge temperature the yeast nearly stops but enzymatic activity continues - starches become sugars, gluten relaxes. Forty-eight hours cold beats four hours warm in flavor, browning, and stretchability, every single time.
Time is an ingredient. A 48-72 hour cold ferment builds flavors a same-day dough cannot have, and the extra sugars are why well-fermented crust browns and blisters so beautifully.

Fridge fermentation is not just storage, and it does not kill the yeast - it slows it. At around 4 degrees Celsius the yeast idles for 24 to 72 hours while enzymes keep converting starch to sugar and building flavor compounds. That is why a two-day dough browns deeper, blisters more, tastes faintly tangy and stretches without a fight. If you change one thing about your pizza, change this.

facts.a: Traditionally, no fridge: the classic Neapolitan method is 8 to 24 hours at room temperature - a first bulk rise, then proofing in dough balls. The STG spec is built around ambient fermentation. Cold fermentation is the modern, and in my view excellent, deviation - but in Naples, nonna's dough never saw a refrigerator.
alt: The tradition is room-temperature all the way: a couple of hours in bulk, then 6-20 hours as balls, timed by the pizzaiolo's experience against the weather. The refrigerator is a modern tool - useful, but not how the canon was written.

The claim that Naples pizzerias all cold ferment for 72 hours is a modern projection, not the tradition. The STG method is ambient: 8 to 24 hours at room temperature, a short bulk rise and then a long proof as balls, with the pizzaiolo reading the weather to time it. Cold fermentation is a fine modern tool, and I use it, but it is the deviation, not the canon.

Room temperature, traditionally - no refrigerator in the picture. A couple of hours in bulk, then 6 to 20 hours as balls, adjusted by feel to the season. That is not a worse version of cold fermentation, it is a different one: shorter, warmer, and built on the pizzaiolo's judgment instead of a thermostat. Both routes make superb pizza when the timing is right.

facts.a: A poolish is a wet preferment: equal weights of flour and water with a pinch of yeast, left 12 to 16 hours before mixing into the final dough. It brings fermented flavor, extensibility, and lively bubbles. It's a French technique the pizza world happily stole - a shortcut to long-ferment character without holding the whole dough that long.
alt: 100 percent hydration preferment - flour, equal water, a whisper of yeast, overnight on the counter. Fold it into your final dough the next day. You get depth of flavor and a silky, extensible dough; very fashionable in contemporary Neapolitan circles.

Not stiff, not Italian, not a sourdough starter: a poolish is the wet preferment, and it runs on commercial yeast. Equal weights of flour and water, a pinch of yeast, 12 to 16 hours on the counter, then mixed into the final dough. It gives you an extensible, bubbly dough with real fermented depth. The stiff Italian cousin at half the water is the biga.

Think of it as a liquid head start. The night before, whisk together equal flour and water with a whisper of yeast and leave it 12 to 16 hours; by morning it is bubbly and smells faintly of beer. Fold that into your final dough and you get long-ferment flavor and a silky stretch without holding all the dough overnight. French in origin, adopted wholesale by contemporary pizzaioli.

facts.a: Biga is the Italian preferment: stiff, around 45 to 50 percent hydration, fermented 16 to 48 hours. Compared to the wetter poolish it favors strength and a more acetic, complex aroma, where poolish favors extensibility and milder sweetness. Modern 'biga 100%' pizza doughs build the entire dough from matured biga - the airiest cornicioni in Italy right now come from that school.

No - the wet French preferment is the poolish, not the biga. Biga is the Italian one, stiff at 45 to 50 percent hydration, matured 16 to 48 hours until it smells sharp and complex. Where poolish buys extensibility and mild sweetness, biga buys strength and an acetic, deeper aroma. The 'biga 100%' doughs behind Italy's puffiest cornicioni are built entirely from that matured stiff dough.

Half the water of a poolish and a completely different result, so no, they are not interchangeable. Biga at 45-50 percent hydration ferments 16 to 48 hours and comes out strong, tangy and structured - exactly what a super-open canotto crust needs to hold its huge air pockets. The current wave of high-percentage biga doughs is the most exciting thing in Italian pizza right now.

facts.a: Absolutely - lievito madre predates commercial yeast, so in a sense sourdough pizza is the older tradition. A stiff Italian starter gives gentle acidity and superb keeping quality. The craft challenge: sourdough ferments less predictably, so timing the balls for service takes real skill. Expect a slightly tangier, chewier crust than with baker's yeast.
alt: Yes, and beautifully. Naturally leavened pizza has more aromatic depth and often better digestibility. Just respect that a starter runs on its own schedule - the margin between perfectly proofed and over the hill is narrower than with commercial yeast.

Sourdough pizza is not a hipster invention - lievito madre, the Italian natural starter, was leavening dough long before commercial yeast existed, so it is the older tradition. A stiff starter gives soft acidity, deeper aroma and a crust that keeps well. The catch is timing: a starter runs on its own clock, so hitting the perfect proof for service takes practice. Expect a slightly tangier, chewier crust.

Use it, and do not believe anyone who says real pizza always means baker's yeast. Naturally leavened pizza has more aromatic depth and many people digest it better. Manage the sourness by keeping the starter stiff and young, and give yourself margin on timing - the window between perfectly proofed and over the hill is narrower than with commercial yeast. The reward is a chewier, more flavorful crust.

facts.a: Less than people think. Mix until the dough comes together, rest it twenty minutes, and a few gentle folds will develop more gluten than aggressive kneading - time and hydration do the work. Ten minutes of moderate hand kneading is plenty for a classic dough; no-knead with stretch-and-folds over an evening works wonderfully for wetter doughs.
alt: Gluten develops through time as much as through work. Mix, rest, then two or three rounds of stretch-and-fold beat fifteen minutes of punishment. Overworked dough tightens up and fights you at stretching time.

Fifteen minutes of kneading is not required, and more is not better. Gluten develops from hydration and time as much as from work: mix until it comes together, rest twenty minutes, then a few folds will do more than a punishing knead. Ten minutes of moderate hand kneading is plenty for a classic dough. Overwork it and it tightens up and snaps back when you try to stretch.

Your tough dough is overworked, not underworked. Kneading builds gluten but it also tightens it, and a long hard session leaves you with a rubber band. Try this: mix, rest twenty minutes, then two or three rounds of stretch-and-fold over an hour. For wetter doughs a no-knead routine of folds across an evening gives a better crumb than any amount of muscle.

Four hundred grams is far too much for a Neapolitan - that is a thick bready disc, not a pizza. Neapolitan balls run 200 to 280 grams for a 22-35 centimeter pie, and the STG spec itself says 180-250. Roman tonda goes lighter still, 180-200 grams, because the disc is rolled thin. Divide at least four hours before baking so the balls relax.

Two hundred to two hundred eighty grams for a Neapolitan, with 250 my pick for a 30 cm pizza; 180 to 200 grams for a Roman tonda of the same diameter, since it is rolled thinner. A bigger ball is not better, it is just a thicker, doughier base. Ball them four hours or more ahead - a freshly balled dough is a rubber band.

q: How do I know if pizza dough is overproofed?

Isn't a longer proof always better, so you can't really overproof?

facts.a: Overproofed dough looks slack and deflated, smells sharply alcoholic or sour, tears instead of stretching, and won't spring in the oven - the yeast has eaten the sugars, so the crust bakes pale and flat. Slightly overproofed dough can still make a decent pan pizza; for a round pizza it's a lost cause, so start over or lower your expectations for the evening.
alt: The tells: it's lost its dome, it smells like a brewery, it feels fragile and tears at the edges when stretched, and it bakes pale because the sugars are gone. Underproofed fights you; overproofed gives up. Both miss the blistered rim.

Dough that tears at the edges is not asking for more time - that is overproofing, not underproofing. Overproofed dough has lost its dome, smells sharply of alcohol, feels fragile and slack, and bakes pale and flat because the yeast has already eaten the sugars. Underproofed dough does the opposite: it snaps back. If yours tears, do not wait longer; make a pan pizza of it or start again.

You absolutely can overproof, and a longer proof is not always better. The signs are unmistakable once you know them: a deflated, spreading ball, a brewery smell, a surface that tears rather than stretches, and no oven spring - the crust comes out pale and flat because the sugars are gone. Slightly over is salvageable as a pan pizza; badly over is a fresh start.

q: What happens with underproofed pizza dough?
Why does my pizza dough snap back when stretching?
Why is my crust dense?
Underproofed dough symptoms?
underproofed pizza dough symptoms
My dough keeps shrinking back every time I push it out. What's going on?
My friend says snap-back means the dough has overproofed. Is he right?
Isn't a dense chewy rim just what a rustic pizza is supposed to be like?
Is snap-back a sign of underproofing or overproofing?
Why does my pizza get one giant bubble and a bready rim?
Tell me how to tell an underproofed dough ball from a ready one.
The dough go back small when I stretch it, why this happen?
What should I do with dough that isn't ready yet?
So dough that resists stretching has gone too far and should be thrown out, right?
How do I know when dough is ready to stretch?
facts.a: Underproofed dough fights back: it resists stretching, snaps back like elastic, and bakes into a dense, bready cornicione with big ugly bubbles instead of an even honeycomb. If the dough won't hold its shape when you push it out, give the balls another hour or two in a warm spot before trying again.
alt: Snap-back is the classic sign - the gluten hasn't relaxed and fermentation hasn't done its work. The bake makes it worse: dense rim, pale color, sometimes one giant balloon bubble. Patience is the fix; dough tells you when it's ready by holding the stretch.

Your friend has it backwards: snap-back is underproofing, not overproofing. An underproofed ball resists stretching, springs back like elastic, and bakes into a dense, bready rim with one or two giant bubbles instead of an even honeycomb. Overproofed dough would tear and go slack instead. The fix is patience: give the balls another hour or two somewhere warm and try again.

Do not throw it out - dough that resists you simply is not ready. The gluten has not relaxed and fermentation has not built the gas yet, so it snaps back and would bake dense and pale. A ready ball feels supple and slightly airy, holds the stretch when you push it out, and does not shrink back. Warm spot, another hour or two, then it will cooperate.

q: How do you stretch Neapolitan pizza dough?
What's the right way to shape a pizza base?
How do pizzaiolos stretch dough so thin?
Can I use a rolling pin on pizza dough?
stretch pizza dough by hand technique
I keep tearing my dough when I try to stretch it thin. How should I be doing it?
My friend says a rolling pin is the proper Italian way to shape pizza. Is he right?
Isn't it easier to just roll the dough out flat with a pin?
Do you press from the center or from the edge when opening a pizza?
Why do Neapolitan pizzaiolos never touch the rim of the dough?
Teach me the Neapolitan stretch, step by step.
How I make the pizza base big without breaking it, the way the pizzaiolo does?
Why is the rolling pin fine in Rome but not in Naples?
So rolling pins are banned for every kind of Italian pizza, right?
What is the slap technique for pizza dough?
facts.a: For Neapolitan: press from the center outward with fingertips, pushing the gas toward the rim, then drape and rotate the disc over your knuckles to widen it - never touching the cornicione. A rolling pin is banned in Naples because it crushes the rim's gas. In Rome, though, the pin is standard: the tonda is meant to be flat and even, with no puffy edge to protect.
alt: The Neapolitan way: fingertips push from the middle out, preserving the rim, then a gentle stretch over the backs of your hands - the 'slap' technique once you're confident. Rolling pins crush the cornicione, which is a crime in Naples but the whole point in Rome.

A rolling pin is not the proper way to shape a Neapolitan - it crushes the gas you spent a day building into the rim. Press with fingertips from the center outward, pushing the air toward the edge and never touching the cornicione, then drape the disc over your knuckles and rotate it wider. Rome is the exception: the tonda is meant to be flat and even, and there the pin is standard.

Center out, edge untouched, and no pin - for Naples. Fingertips flatten the middle and push the gas into the rim, then the disc stretches over the backs of your hands, rotating as you go; the slap technique is the show-off version of the same move. Rolling pins are not banned for every Italian pizza, though: the Roman tonda is rolled flat on purpose, because it has no puffy rim to protect.

q: What flour should I use for dusting when shaping pizza?
Why use semolina to stretch pizza?
What's the best bench flour for pizza?
How do I stop pizza dough sticking when shaping?
bench flour semolina pizza
My pizza bases keep sticking to the peel. What should I dust with?
My friend says cornmeal is the traditional Italian dusting for pizza. Is he right?
Isn't plain flour fine for dusting the bench?
Should I use semolina or cornmeal under the pizza?
Why does the bottom of my pizza taste burnt and bitter?
Tell me what to dust the bench and peel with and how much.
What flour I put on the table so the pizza not stick?
What is semola rimacinata?
So cornmeal is what real pizzerias use on the peel, right?
Why does semolina work better than flour for shaping?
facts.a: Coarse semolina (semola rimacinata) is the classic bench flour: it acts like ball bearings under the dough, doesn't absorb into it, and toasts nutty rather than burning bitter in the oven. Plain flour works but burns faster; cornmeal is an American habit that scorches at Neapolitan temperatures. Whatever you use, brush the excess off before launching.
alt: Semola rimacinata - fine-ground durum. It keeps the dough gliding, adds a faint crunch to the underside, and tolerates heat far better than soft wheat flour. Excess bench flour on the oven floor turns to soot, so dust with intent, not enthusiasm.

Cornmeal is not the Italian tradition - it is an American pizzeria habit, and at Neapolitan temperatures it scorches into bitter grit. Italians dust with semola rimacinata, fine-ground durum semolina: it rolls under the dough like ball bearings, does not soak in, and toasts nutty rather than burning. Plain flour works in a pinch but burns faster. Brush off the excess before you launch.

Use semolina, and use it sparingly. The bitter burnt taste on your base is almost always excess dusting flour carbonizing on the oven floor - plain flour and especially cornmeal go black fast at pizza heat. Semola rimacinata tolerates the heat, adds a whisper of crunch underneath, and keeps the dough gliding while you shape. Dust, shape, then brush the surplus off the peel.

q: What is autolyse in pizza dough?
Should I autolyse my pizza dough?
How does an autolyse rest work?
autolyse pizza dough
I've heard bread bakers rest flour and water before kneading. Does that help pizza dough?
My friend says autolyse means mixing everything and letting it rest. Is he right?
Isn't a rest before kneading just wasted time?
Do I add the salt and yeast before or after the autolyse?
How long should an autolyse be for pizza?
Explain what an autolyse does to the dough and why I'd bother.
The autolyse, I mix only flour and water, or all the ingredients?
Why does my strong flour dough come together so easily after a rest?
So autolyse is just resting the finished dough, right?
What's the point of resting flour and water before adding salt?
facts.a: Autolyse is a rest right after mixing just the flour and water - twenty minutes to an hour before adding salt and yeast. The flour hydrates fully and enzymes begin developing gluten on their own, so the dough comes together with less kneading and stretches more willingly. Cheap trick, real payoff, especially with strong flours.
alt: Mix flour and water, walk away for half an hour, then add the rest. The dough practically kneads itself - hydration and enzymes do quietly what your hands would do loudly. Particularly worth it for high-W flours that otherwise fight you.

Resting the finished dough is not an autolyse - an autolyse rests only the flour and water, before the salt and yeast go in. Twenty minutes to an hour is plenty. In that time the flour hydrates fully and its own enzymes start building gluten, so the dough comes together with far less kneading and stretches willingly later. Add salt and yeast afterwards, mix briefly, and carry on.

Not wasted time at all - it is the laziest gluten development there is. Stir flour and water into a shaggy mass, cover it, and leave it twenty minutes to an hour with no salt and no yeast. When you come back the dough is smoother and more extensible than kneading would have made it. It pays off most with strong, high-W flours that otherwise resist you.

q: What temperature should pizza dough be?
Does dough temperature matter?
Why is my dough fermenting too fast?
What's the ideal final dough temperature?
final dough temperature pizza
It's a hot summer kitchen and my dough is racing ahead of schedule. What do I do?
My friend says warmer dough is always better because it rises faster. Is he right?
Isn't the water temperature irrelevant since it all ends up at room temperature anyway?
Should I use cold or warm water for pizza dough?
How much does temperature change fermentation speed?
Give me a dough temperature target and a simple way to hit it at home.
What temperature the dough should have when I finish mixing?
Why do professionals measure their water temperature for dough?
So warmer is better for pizza dough fermentation, right?
How do I slow down fermentation in a warm kitchen?
facts.a: Aim for a final dough temperature around 23 to 25 degrees Celsius. Warmer, and fermentation races ahead of flavor; the classic fix is using cold water on a hot day. Professionals calculate water temperature from flour and room temperature - at home, just remember: hot kitchen, cold water; cold kitchen, lukewarm water.
alt: Around 24 degrees at the end of mixing is the target. Fermentation speed roughly doubles per 8 degrees, so a summer kitchen can wreck a schedule. Water temperature is your thermostat - it's the one ingredient whose temperature you fully control.

Warmer is not better, only faster, and fast fermentation skips the flavor. Aim for a final dough temperature of 23 to 25 degrees Celsius; every 8 degrees warmer roughly doubles the speed, so a summer kitchen can turn a 24-hour plan into a 12-hour one. Water is your thermostat: cold water in a hot kitchen, lukewarm in a cold one. Professionals calculate it; at home a thermometer and that rule are enough.

Use cold water on a hot day. The dough leaves the mixer at whatever temperature your flour, room and water average to, and that number decides your whole schedule - 23 to 25 degrees Celsius is the target. Water temperature matters precisely because it is the one ingredient you fully control. Too warm and the yeast races ahead of flavor; too cool and you simply wait a little longer.

q: Can I stretch pizza dough straight from the fridge?
Why does cold dough resist stretching?
How long should dough warm up before shaping?
cold pizza dough won't stretch
I took the dough out of the fridge and it keeps snapping back. Is it underproofed?
My friend says you should shape the dough cold because it's easier to handle. Is he right?
Isn't it fine to stretch straight from the fridge if the dough has fermented long enough?
Is cold dough snapping back a temperature problem or a proofing problem?
How long before baking should I take the dough balls out of the fridge?
Tell me how to prep cold-fermented dough balls for stretching.
The dough from fridge is very hard to stretch, what I do?
How should a dough ball feel when it's ready to shape?
So dough should be shaped straight from the fridge, right?
Why do cold-fermented balls need to warm up before shaping?
facts.a: Don't stretch fridge-cold dough - cold gluten is tight gluten, and it will snap back or tear. Take the balls out one and a half to three hours before baking so they return toward room temperature and relax. This is the most common home mistake after underproofing, and the easiest to fix: it costs only planning.
alt: Cold dough is a rubber band. Give the balls two hours or so on the counter after the fridge; they should feel supple and slightly airy when you press them. The stretch then happens almost by itself.

Never shape it cold, whatever anyone tells you about it being easier to handle. Cold gluten is tight gluten: a fridge-cold ball snaps back, tears and refuses to go thin. Take the balls out one and a half to three hours before baking and let them come toward room temperature until they feel supple and slightly airy. Only then does the stretch happen without a fight.

Snap-back straight out of the fridge is usually a temperature problem, not a proofing one. Long fermentation does not exempt a ball from needing to warm up - the gluten relaxes as it comes toward room temperature, and that takes about two hours on the counter. Press a ball: if it feels supple and springs back slowly it is ready; if it is firm and cold, give it more time.

q: Which one controls fermentation speed, the salt or the yeast?
Salt and yeast in pizza dough - which is 2.5 to 3 percent and which is a couple of grams?
I always mix up the salt and yeast amounts. Which one is the tiny one?
My friend says the yeast should be 3 percent of the flour. Is he right?
Isn't yeast the ingredient that makes the dough taste salty and strong?
Is it the salt or the yeast that slows fermentation?
What do salt and yeast each do in pizza dough?
Explain the roles of salt and yeast in the dough and give me both numbers.
salt vs yeast pizza dough amounts
Salt and yeast, which one I put more of in pizza dough?
So yeast is the big number and salt is the pinch, right?
Which ingredient tightens the gluten, salt or yeast?
For one kilo of flour, how much salt and how much yeast?
facts.a: Two different jobs, two very different amounts. Yeast makes the gas: it ferments the sugars and raises the dough, and you want only one to three grams of fresh yeast per kilo of flour for a long ferment. Salt is the brake and the backbone: it slows that yeast down and tightens the gluten, and it goes in at 2.5 to 3 percent - 25 to 30 grams per kilo. The big number is the salt; the pinch is the yeast.
alt: People flip these constantly, so let me be blunt: the yeast is not 3 percent, the salt is. Salt goes in at 2.5 to 3 percent of flour weight, 25 to 30 grams per kilo, and its job is to season, firm the gluten and slow fermentation. Yeast goes in at one to three grams per kilo - a pea-sized amount - and its job is to produce the gas. Yeast drives; salt brakes.

The yeast is the accelerator and the salt is the brake. Yeast ferments the sugars and inflates the dough, which is why a slow Neapolitan dough uses only one to three grams of fresh yeast per kilo of flour. Salt reins that yeast in and tightens the gluten so the dough stretches thin, and it needs a real quantity: 25 to 30 grams per kilo, 2.5 to 3 percent. Never swap those two numbers.

Salt is the one that slows fermentation, not the yeast - the yeast is what causes it. For a kilo of flour you use 25 to 30 grams of salt, which is 2.5 to 3 percent, and only one to three grams of fresh yeast. Yeast makes the gas; salt seasons, strengthens the gluten and keeps the yeast from running away. If you remember one thing: salt is grams by the spoonful, yeast is grams by the pinch.

q: Is the W number the same as the protein percentage?
Is it the W number or the protein percentage I should look at when buying flour?
My friend says W300 means 30 percent protein. Is he right?
Isn't W just another way of writing protein content?
W strength vs protein content - what's the difference?
My flour bag shows 12.5 percent protein but no W. Can I work out the W from that?
Explain the difference between flour strength and protein percentage.
w index versus protein percent flour
The W number and the protein, it is same thing or different?
So W300 flour is 30 percent protein, right?
Why do two flours with the same protein have different W values?
What does W measure that protein percentage doesn't?
facts.a: They are related but they are not the same thing. Protein percentage is a chemical count of how much protein the flour contains - pizza flours sit around 11 to 13 percent. W is a mechanical test: the Chopin alveograph inflates a dough bubble and measures the work to burst it, giving W 200-250 for same-day doughs up to W 280-320 for two-day ferments. Protein is the raw material; W is how well that protein actually performs. W300 does not mean 30 percent protein.
alt: No - W300 is not 30 percent protein, and W is not a protein figure at all. Protein percentage tells you how much gluten-forming protein is in the bag, typically 11 to 13 percent for pizza flour. W tells you how that gluten behaves under strain, measured by blowing a bubble of dough in an alveograph. Two flours at 12.5 percent protein can test at quite different W, because quality of gluten matters as much as quantity.

Look at W if the bag gives it; fall back to protein if it does not, but know they are different measures. Protein percentage is quantity - 11 to 13 percent is the pizza range. W is performance - the alveograph's measure of dough strength and fermentation tolerance, W 200-250 for short doughs, 280-320 for 24-48 hours. You cannot calculate one exactly from the other, only estimate.

Different things, and mixing them up is the most common flour mistake I hear. Protein content is a percentage of the flour's weight; for pizza you want roughly 11 to 13. W is a strength index from the Chopin alveograph, a number like 250 or 320 that describes how much work the gluten can take and therefore how long the dough can ferment. High protein usually means higher W, but the W is what actually predicts the dough's behavior.

q: Which is wetter, Neapolitan dough or Roman dough?
Neapolitan vs Roman hydration - what are the numbers?
I'm choosing between a Neapolitan and a Roman tonda dough. How does the water differ?
My friend says Roman pizza dough is wetter than Neapolitan because it's crispier. Is he right?
Isn't all Italian pizza dough roughly the same hydration?
Is Neapolitan hydration higher or lower than Roman tonda?
Compare the hydration of Neapolitan, Roman tonda and Roman al taglio.
hydration neapolitan roman tonda al taglio compare
How much water in Neapolitan dough and how much in Roman dough, which one more?
So Neapolitan and Roman use the same dough, just baked differently, right?
Which Italian pizza style uses the wettest dough?
Give me the hydration for each Italian style in one answer.
facts.a: Three styles, three numbers. Neapolitan sits at 55 to 62 percent hydration - soft from the fierce 90-second bake, not from water. Roman tonda is the driest at around 55 percent, with a little oil, rolled thin and baked longer for crunch. Roman al taglio is the wet one, 75 to 90 percent, baked in trays for an open, airy crumb. So Neapolitan is a touch wetter than tonda, and al taglio is wetter than both.
alt: Roman tonda is not wetter than Neapolitan - it is drier, and that dryness is where the crunch comes from. Tonda runs about 55 percent hydration plus oil; Neapolitan runs 55 to 62 percent; and only Roman al taglio goes truly wet, at 75 to 90 percent for a tray-baked, open crumb. Crispiness comes from low water and a long bake, not from a wet dough.

Not the same dough at all. Neapolitan: 55-62 percent water, no oil, 90 seconds in a 450-degree oven. Roman tonda: around 55 percent, a spoonful of oil, rolled flat and baked longer for a cracker snap. Roman al taglio: 75-90 percent, high-hydration tray pizza with a honeycomb crumb. Same country, three philosophies, and the hydration number is the quickest way to tell them apart.

The wettest is al taglio by a mile, at 75 to 90 percent. Neapolitan is in the middle at 55 to 62 percent, though people wrongly imagine it higher because the crust is so soft. Roman tonda is the driest at roughly 55 percent with oil. If someone tells you all Italian pizza dough is about the same hydration, hand them a scrocchiarella and a slice of al taglio and let them feel the difference.

q: What's the difference between a poolish and a biga?
Poolish or biga - which is the wet one?
I keep mixing up poolish and biga. Can you set them side by side?
My friend says poolish and biga are just two names for the same preferment. Is he right?
Isn't a biga just a poolish made the Italian way?
Which should I use for pizza, poolish or biga, and why?
Compare poolish and biga in hydration, time and what they do to the dough.
poolish biga difference pizza
The poolish and the biga, what is different between them?
So poolish is the stiff Italian one and biga is the wet French one, right?
Which preferment gives more extensibility, and which gives more strength?
Which preferment do the canotto pizzerias use?
facts.a: Poolish is wet, biga is stiff - that is the whole distinction. A poolish is equal weights of flour and water with a pinch of yeast, 12 to 16 hours, French in origin, and it gives extensibility, lively bubbles and a mild sweetness. A biga is Italian, around 45 to 50 percent hydration, matured 16 to 48 hours, and it gives strength and a sharper, more complex aroma. Want a silky, easy stretch? Poolish. Want a huge, structured canotto rim? Biga.
alt: They are not two names for one thing, and they are not the way round people often say. The poolish is the wet one - 100 percent hydration, French, 12-16 hours, for extensibility and gentle flavor. The biga is the stiff one - Italian, 45-50 percent hydration, 16-48 hours, for strength and an acetic, deep aroma. The airiest cornicioni in Italy right now come from high-percentage biga doughs.

Wrong way round: the biga is stiff and Italian, the poolish is wet and French. Poolish - flour and equal water, whisper of yeast, overnight - buys you a silky, extensible dough with mild sweetness. Biga - roughly half the water, 16 to 48 hours - buys you dough strength and a more complex, slightly sour aroma. Both are valid; pick by what your crust is missing.

Think water and time. Poolish: equal flour and water, 12 to 16 hours, gives extensibility and bubbles. Biga: 45 to 50 percent hydration, 16 to 48 hours, gives structure and a sharper, richer aroma. A biga is not simply an Italian poolish; the low hydration ferments differently and builds strength a poolish never will. That is why the super-open canotto school runs on biga rather than poolish.

q: How do I tell overproofed from underproofed pizza dough?
Overproofed or underproofed - which one snaps back and which one tears?
My dough isn't behaving and I can't tell if it's had too much time or too little. How do I know?
My friend says a dense rim means the dough was overproofed. Is he right?
Isn't a pale crust always a sign of underproofing?
Is snap-back overproofing or underproofing, and is tearing the other one?
Put the signs of overproofed and underproofed dough side by side for me.
overproofed vs underproofed pizza dough signs
My dough have problem but I don't know if too much ferment or not enough, how I know?
So dough that tears is underproofed and dough that snaps back is overproofed, right?
Which proofing mistake can I still fix, and which one is a lost cause?
Both my underproofed and overproofed pizzas lacked a blistered rim - how do I tell which problem I had?
facts.a: Underproofed dough fights you; overproofed dough gives up. Underproofed: it snaps back when stretched, feels tight, and bakes into a dense, bready rim with big ugly bubbles - the fix is more time in a warm spot. Overproofed: it has lost its dome, smells sharply alcoholic, tears instead of stretching, and bakes pale and flat because the sugars are gone - no fix, only a pan pizza or a fresh batch. Dense means under; slack and torn means over.
alt: A dense rim is not overproofing - it is underproofing, so your friend has it backwards. Underproofed dough is tight and elastic, snaps back, and bakes dense with one giant bubble. Overproofed dough is the opposite: slack, deflated, smelling of a brewery, tearing at the edges and baking pale because the yeast has eaten all the sugar. Under is fixable with another hour or two; over is not.

Snap-back is under, tearing is over - not the other way round. A ball that resists stretching and springs back has not relaxed or fermented enough; give it time and warmth. A ball that spreads, smells alcoholic and rips when you push it out has gone too far and will not spring in the oven. Both miss the blistered cornicione, but only the underproofed one can still be rescued.

Pale is not always underproofing - both mistakes bake pale, so use the feel and the smell instead. Underproofed: tight, springy, snaps back, bakes dense and bready with a few huge bubbles. Overproofed: slack, deflated, brewery smell, tears at the edges, bakes flat with no rise. Tight and shrinking means wait longer; loose and tearing means the moment has passed.

q: Should I cold ferment or ferment at room temperature?
Cold fermentation vs room temperature - which is right for Neapolitan dough?
I want to make pizza tomorrow evening. Fridge or counter for the dough?
My friend says room-temperature fermentation is wrong and only cold fermentation makes real pizza. Is he right?
Isn't cold fermentation just the correct way and room temperature the old-fashioned mistake?
Is cold or ambient fermentation the traditional Neapolitan method, and which is better?
Compare cold fermentation and room-temperature fermentation for pizza dough and tell me when to use each.
cold ferment vs room temperature pizza dough
The dough, I put in fridge or I leave on the table? Which is more correct?
So the fridge is mandatory for proper pizza dough, right?
How long does a room-temperature ferment take versus a cold one?
Can I mix the two, some hours warm and some hours cold?
facts.a: Both are valid - two routes to the same place, and neither is a mistake. Room temperature is the Neapolitan tradition: 8 to 24 hours ambient, bulk then balls, timed by feel; it suits a same-day or next-day plan. Cold fermentation, 24 to 72 hours at around 4 degrees Celsius, is the modern route: deeper flavor, better browning, and a schedule you can hold for days. Baking soon and want the classic method, go warm; want flexibility and flavor, go cold. A few hours warm and then the fridge works beautifully too.
alt: The fridge is not mandatory and room temperature is not a mistake - the STG Neapolitan dough was written around ambient fermentation, 8 to 24 hours with no refrigerator in sight. Cold fermentation is the modern upgrade: 24 to 72 hours at about 4 degrees Celsius buys complexity, browning and a flexible schedule. Use warm when you bake within a day and want the classic method; use cold when you want maximum flavor and time on your side.

Room temperature when you are baking within the day, cold when you can plan ahead. Ambient fermentation - the Naples way, 8 to 24 hours - gives a clean, classic crust and demands attention to the weather. Cold fermentation at around 4 degrees Celsius for 24 to 72 hours idles the yeast while enzymes build flavor and sugars, so the crust browns deeper and tastes richer. I use both; the calendar decides.

Only cold fermentation makes real pizza? No - Naples fermented its dough at room temperature long before anyone owned a refrigerator, and still does. Ambient fermentation runs 8 to 24 hours and is the tradition. Cold fermentation runs 24 to 72 hours at fridge temperature and is the modern refinement, with a real flavor and browning advantage. Pick cold for flavor and flexibility, warm for tradition and speed.
